title: Keep named intermediates for the combining lemma
intent: When golfing a proof whose goal closes by one application of a combining lemma `combine` over two intermediate facts, keep those intermediates as named `have`s (`h1 : A`, `h2 : B`) and close with `exact combine h1 h2`, rather than inlining them into a single opaque `exact combine (...)`: the decomposition into two leaf facts plus the combining application stays visible.

applicability.goal_shape: A proof whose final step is one application of a combining lemma `combine` to two (or more) intermediate facts, where inlining those intermediates into the application would produce a single long or nested term; the intermediates are stated as named `have`s (`h1 : A`, `h2 : B`) and the goal closes by `exact combine h1 h2`.
applicability.use_when: the intermediate facts are meaningful on their own and worth naming for re-reading; the combined application would be long or nested (the file's Bad example is 'obscure nested lambdas spanning 100+ chars', line 248); or a later step must refer back to an earlier fact (the companion 'Don't Remove Helpful Names' rule, lines 256-266).
applicability.avoid_when: the intermediate is short and used exactly once (the file's Tier 3 prescribes inlining single-use `have` terms under 40 chars), the name adds no meaning, or the goal is trivial enough that the named intermediates are noise.

The theorem-scale shape is 3 direct lemmas (`h1`, `h2`, `combine`) with no chain of project lemmas below the main theorem (depth 1): direct_lemmas=3, depth=1, glue_lines=3, child_lines=[1,1,1].
claims.evidence: counted on the copied file: the parent site (lines 251-253) is 3 lines; each child site is its own single line (h1 at 251, h2 at 252, combine at 253); h1 and h2 are independent named `have`s and combine is applied directly, so no project-lemma chain below the parent exceeds length 1.

metrics.how_counted: parent site lines 251-253 (3 lines); child sites h1 (251), h2 (252), combine (253) one line each; h1 and h2 are independent named `have`s and combine is applied directly, so the longest chain of project lemmas below the parent is 1.

consequences: Keeping the intermediates named preserves the dependency structure — which fact feeds which argument of `combine` — at the cost of two extra `have` lines versus the inlined one-liner. The companion obligation is that a later step can use an earlier fact only if that fact was named first: an anonymous `have : ...` cannot be cited (the 'Don't Remove Helpful Names' Bad example shows a second anonymous `have` silently depending on the first, lines 259-261). Failure modes: naming an intermediate that is never used again leaves a dead binding the golfer's Tier 3 would inline; inlining a fact that a later step needs breaks the proof.
